# 1. Notebooks

## Google Colab

In your browser:

1. Keep these slides open in one tab to copy from
2. In another tab, go to <https://colab.research.google.com>
   - Sign in with your DCU or personal Google account
   - File → New notebook

. . .

Nothing to install. It runs on Google's machines and saves to your Drive.

## How a Notebook Works

A notebook is a sequence of **cells**.

- **Code cells** run Python and show the output beneath
- **Text cells** hold markdown: your commentary, which is not optional

. . .

`Shift + Enter` runs the current cell and moves to the next.

## The One Thing That Will Bite You

Cells run **in the order you run them**, not in the order they appear.

. . .

A notebook that works for you may not work for the person you send it to,
because you ran cell 8 before cell 5.

. . .

**Before you submit anything: Runtime → Restart and run all.** If it fails, it
was never working.

## Documenting as You Go

The notebook is the audit trail we formalise in Lecture 15.

. . .

Every analysis cell gets a text cell above it saying **what question it answers**,
and a text cell below saying **what you concluded**.

. . .

A notebook of 40 code cells and no prose is not an analysis, it is a transcript.

# 2. pandas

## Importing

```{.python}
import pandas as pd
```

. . .

`pd` is the universal alias. Every example you find online assumes it.

## The DataFrame

A DataFrame is a table: named columns, indexed rows, each column one type.

. . .

Think of a well-behaved spreadsheet with the following rules enforced:

- Every column has one name
- Every column holds one kind of thing
- Every row is one observation

. . .

That last point is the definition of tidy data, and your GA4 export mostly obeys it.

## Loading Your Export

From a file you uploaded to Colab:

```{.python}
ga4 = pd.read_csv("ga4_export.csv")
```

. . .

From a URL, which is more reproducible:

```{.python}
ga4 = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/user/repo/main/ga4_export.csv")
```

. . .

GA4 CSV exports carry several header lines before the table. Skip them:

```{.python}
ga4 = pd.read_csv("ga4_export.csv", skiprows=9)
```

## Looking at It First

Always, in this order:

```{.python}
ga4.shape       # (rows, columns)
ga4.head()      # first five rows
ga4.dtypes      # what type is each column
ga4.info()      # types plus non-null counts
ga4.describe()  # numeric summaries
```

. . .

`ga4.dtypes` is the one people skip and regret. A date read as text, or sessions
read as text because of a thousands separator, will silently break everything
downstream.

## Fixing Types

```{.python}
ga4["date"] = pd.to_datetime(ga4["date"], format="%Y%m%d")
ga4["sessions"] = pd.to_numeric(ga4["sessions"], errors="coerce")
```

. . .

`errors="coerce"` turns unparseable values into `NaN` rather than raising.
Then count them, because a silent `NaN` is a lie:

```{.python}
ga4["sessions"].isna().sum()
```

# 3. Selecting and Filtering

## Columns

```{.python}
ga4["sessions"]                          # one column, a Series
ga4[["date", "sessions", "channel"]]     # several columns, a DataFrame
```

. . .

Single brackets give you a Series, double brackets give you a DataFrame. This
distinction causes more confusion than it should.

## Rows

Filtering uses a boolean condition:

```{.python}
ga4[ga4["channel"] == "Organic Search"]
ga4[ga4["sessions"] > 10]
```

. . .

Combine with `&` (and) and `|` (or), **with brackets around each condition**:

```{.python}
ga4[(ga4["channel"] == "Organic Search") & (ga4["sessions"] > 10)]
```

. . .

Python's `and` / `or` do not work here. This is not negotiable and it is not
your fault.

## Chaining

The readable pattern, which is the one we will keep using:

```{.python}
(ga4
  .query("channel == 'Organic Search'")
  .sort_values("sessions", ascending=False)
  .head(10)
)
```

. . .

Wrap the chain in brackets, one operation per line. Read it top to bottom as a
sentence.

## New Columns

```{.python}
ga4 = ga4.assign(
    conversion_rate = lambda d: d["key_events"] / d["sessions"],
    is_mobile = lambda d: d["device"] == "mobile"
)
```

. . .

`assign` with a `lambda` keeps the chain intact and avoids modifying the
original object in place, which is what makes a notebook reproducible.

## A First Summary

```{.python}
(ga4
  .groupby("channel")
  .agg(sessions=("sessions", "sum"),
       key_events=("key_events", "sum"))
  .assign(cvr=lambda d: d["key_events"] / d["sessions"])
  .sort_values("sessions", ascending=False)
)
```

. . .

We take `groupby` properly next lecture. For now, notice it is the same
split-apply-combine idea as a Tableau breakdown, written down.

# 4. A Note on Libraries

## pandas, polars, and what you will meet

This module uses **pandas**, because it is what marketing teams, tutorials and
AI assistants all assume.

. . .

You will meet **polars** elsewhere (including in BAA1030). It is faster and its
syntax is arguably cleaner. The concepts transfer directly: filter, select,
with_columns, group_by, agg.

. . .

Learning the ideas matters more than learning the library. The library will
change.

# 5. Vibe Coding with pandas

## AI This Block: Agentic Coding

Where we are on the module's AI spine, introduced in Lecture 10:

> **The assistant writes and runs the code with you.**

Lecture 10 covered the modes and the verification discipline. This section is
the pandas-specific version.

## What Vibe Coding Is

Describing the transformation you want in words and letting an assistant write
the pandas.

. . .

It works well here because:

- The chained syntax reads top to bottom, so it is easy to verify
- pandas is heavily represented in training data, so the code is usually idiomatic
- You can check the output shape immediately

. . .

It does **not** mean running code you have not checked.

## In Practice

**Step 1:** Describe the goal, naming your data

> "From a pandas DataFrame called `ga4` with columns `date`, `channel`,
> `sessions` and `key_events`, compute sessions and conversion rate per channel
> for the last 8 weeks, sorted by sessions."

. . .

**Step 2:** The assistant produces code

```{.python}
(ga4
  .query("date >= @cutoff")
  .groupby("channel")
  .agg(sessions=("sessions", "sum"),
       key_events=("key_events", "sum"))
  .assign(cvr=lambda d: d.key_events / d.sessions)
  .sort_values("sessions", ascending=False)
)
```

**Step 3:** Read it, run it, check the total against GA4

## Tips

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Good prompts are specific:**

- Name the DataFrame and the exact column names
- Say pandas, or you may get polars or SQL
- State the grain you want out
- Say what to do with missing values

**A good prompt:**

> "Using pandas, on `ga4` with columns `date`, `channel`, `sessions`, add a
> column `week` from `date` and return sessions per channel per week as a wide
> table."
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Common pitfalls:**

- Not naming the library, so you get a different one
- Column names that do not match your export
- Accepting a `SettingWithCopyWarning` without reading it
- Chained operations that silently drop rows

**Always check:**

- Did the row count change when it should not have?
- Are the totals the same as before the transformation?
- Does one known channel match GA4?
:::
::::

## The pandas-Specific Trap

<!-- Speaker notes: this is the one that costs students marks, because the
     output looks fine. -->

An assistant will happily write a `groupby` that drops your `NaN` groups without
mentioning it.

. . .

`groupby` excludes missing keys by default. If 15% of your sessions have no
channel recorded, they vanish from the table and the totals no longer reconcile.

. . .

**Check your total against the ungrouped total. Every time.**
